title: The Translator's Dilemma
text:
Literary translation is often described as an act of interpretation rather than mere transference. A translator must reconcile the lexical precision of the source text with the idiomatic expectations of a new readership, and this negotiation rarely yields a perfect equivalent. Idioms, cultural allusions, and the rhythm of a sentence resist direct substitution, so the translator is forced to make deliberate sacrifices. Many critics argue that the most successful translations are those that conceal their own labour and read as if they had been composed originally in the target language.

Yet the question of fidelity remains contentious. Some scholars insist that a translation should foreground its foreignness, preserving unfamiliar syntax so that readers feel the distance of the original. Others contend that such estrangement is a form of intellectual vanity, and that the translator's primary obligation is to the reader's experience of beauty. Both positions reveal an uncomfortable truth: every translation is simultaneously a loss and a creation, and the measure of its success lies in how gracefully it acknowledges both.

questions.text: According to paragraph one, what do many critics say the most successful translations do?
options: They emphasise the foreign syntax of the source text.
They hide the translator's effort and read as if originally written in the target language.
They replace every idiom with a literal equivalent.
They are published without any critical commentary.

questions.text: According to paragraph two, what do some scholars insist a translation should do?
options: Foreground its foreignness by preserving unfamiliar syntax.
Remove all unfamiliar expressions so the text is easy to read.
Prioritise the translator's own reputation above the author's words.
Avoid any loss of meaning entirely.

questions.text: What can be inferred about the translator's role from the passage as a whole?
options: It is mechanical and requires no personal judgement.
It involves creative decisions that cannot be avoided.
It is identical to writing an original work.
It matters only to scholars, not to ordinary readers.

questions.text: Why does the author describe the 'uncomfortable truth' in paragraph two as uncomfortable?
options: Because readers never notice the differences between texts.
Because critics refuse to discuss the question at all.
Because it suggests that no translation can be fully faithful, yet every translation still has value.
Because publishers always reject translations that depart from the original.

paragraph_translations: Edebi çeviri çoğu zaman yalnızca aktarma değil, bir yorumlama eylemi olarak tanımlanır. Çevirmen, kaynak metnin sözcüksel kesinliğini yeni bir okurun deyimsel beklentileriyle uzlaştırmak zorundadır ve bu pazarlık nadiren mükemmel bir karşılık doğurur. Deyimler, kültürel göndermeler ve cümlenin ritmi doğrudan ikame edilmeye direnir; bu yüzden çevirmen bilinçli fedakârlıklar yapmak zorunda kalır. Birçok eleştirmen, en başarılı çevirilerin kendi emeklerini gizleyen ve sanki hedef dilde özgün olarak yazılmış gibi okunanlar olduğunu savunur.

Yine de sadakat sorusu tartışmalı olmayı sürdürür. Bazı akademisyenler, bir çevirinin yabancılığını öne çıkarması gerektiğini, okura orijinalin uzaklığını hissettirmek için alışılmadık sözdizimini koruması gerektiğini ısrarla savunur. Diğerleri ise bu tür yabancılaştırmanın entelektüel bir kibir olduğunu ve çevirmenin asıl yükümlülüğünün okurun güzelliği deneyimlemesine olduğunu öne sürer. Her iki görüş de rahatsız edici bir gerçeği ortaya koyar: her çeviri aynı anda hem bir kayıp hem de bir yaratıdır ve başarısının ölçüsü, her ikisini de ne kadar zarifçe kabul ettiğinde yatar.
